title: Detection of Acquire Infrastructure
summary: This strategy detects adversary acquisition of infrastructure, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1583 (Acquire Infrastructure). The technique covers the whole shopping list: domains, servers, virtual private servers, cloud accounts, web services, and even business relationships bought or rented to support an operation. From a defender's point of view, most of the buying happens in accounts you do not control, so the detection combines external observations with the narrow internal cases that are visible, such as an unknown identity creating cloud compute, a certificate issued for a name that mimics your brand, or a large quantity of new hosts resolving to one registration. Useful telemetry includes cloud audit logs for account and instance creation, certificate transparency and registration feeds, passive domain name system data, and cloud billing or cost anomaly reports. The strategy fails when it is built as a single rule, because acquisition leaves no consistent artefact; it works better as a score across several weak signals reviewed together.

beginner.definition: This detection looks at how attackers obtain the tools of their trade, such as servers, domain names, and cloud accounts. Most of the buying happens on the internet, outside your company. The detection combines outside data with the few internal signs, such as a strange cloud account creating many machines.
beginner.whyItMatters: Everything an attacker does afterwards depends on having somewhere to work from. That work costs money and leaves a paper trail, but the trail is usually outside your view. If you watch the small number of signals you can see, you get warning before any attack reaches your users. You also learn which parts of your cloud estate are open to abuse.
howItWorks: Cloud audit logs record who created an account, started a server, or changed a service setting.
External feeds record new domain names, new certificates, and new hosting ranges.
The detection looks for scale and novelty, such as many servers created by one unknown identity.
It compares new assets with your brand, your staff, and your approved supplier list.
Weak signals are combined into one score, because no single one proves anything.
The analyst reviews the case, blocks the infrastructure where possible, and closes the cloud gap.
beginner.example: Think of a stadium before a match. Security watches the gates, but the planning happens in a warehouse full of hired vans, bought radios, and printed tickets. No single purchase is suspicious. Taken together, and seen days before the match, the shopping list is the warning.
takeaways: Acquisition usually happens outside your network, so look for weak external signals and combine them.
Cloud account and compute creation is one of the few places where you can see preparation directly.
The most useful output is a takedown or a closed cloud gap, not only an alert.

objectives: List the infrastructure categories adversaries acquire and what each is used for later
Identify cloud audit, registration, and certificate telemetry that show acquisition in progress
Write a scored rule that combines weak signals instead of relying on one strong indicator
Detect suspicious cloud provisioning by identity, quantity, region, and creation rate
Turn an acquisition finding into a block, a takedown request, or an internal cloud control fix
dataSources: Cloud provider audit logs for account creation, compute instance launch, storage bucket creation, and service enablement
Cloud billing and cost anomaly reports showing sudden provisioning of many resources in one period
Certificate transparency monitoring for certificates naming the organisation or its brands
Domain registration and passive DNS monitoring showing bulk registration or many hosts on one new registration
Web proxy and DNS resolver logs showing internal clients contacting newly provisioned hosting or file transfer services
logic: The detection combines several weak indicators into one case: a cloud identity that creates resources it has never created before, at an unusual rate or in an unusual region; a certificate issued for a name that resembles your brand; a burst of newly registered domains sharing a registrar or name server; and internal clients newly contacting that infrastructure. The fields that must be correlated are the acting identity and its credential age, the resource type and region, the creation count and rate, the billing account, the certificate or domain subject, and the first internal contact. The benign version is a development team provisioning a batch of instances through an approved pipeline, in a documented region, from an account with history and a change ticket. The malicious version shows a new or rarely used identity, a region the organisation never uses, provisioning immediately after credential creation, and resources that have no name tags matching your standards.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Unusual Cloud Compute Provisioning by New or Unapproved Identity
# logsource:
#   product: aws
#   category: cloud_audit
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event.action|in:
#       - RunInstances
#       - CreateBucket
#       - CreateUser
#       - CreateAccessKey
#   novelty:
#     user.identity_age_days: < 7
#   scale:
#     event.count: > 10 within 30m
#   filter_pipeline:
#     user.name|in: approved_provisioning_roles
#     cloud.region|in: approved_regions
#   condition: (selection and novelty) or (selection and scale) and not filter_pipeline
# level: medium
falsePositives: Development and platform teams running approved autoscaling or batch jobs that create many instances quickly
New cloud accounts created during a legitimate migration or a proof of concept project
Marketing and agency partners registering campaign domains and certificates on your behalf
Security research and red team activity performed under a documented engagement
Vendor trials and free tier signups made by engineers without informing the cloud platform team
tuningNotes: Build an inventory of approved provisioning roles, regions, and naming standards, then filter on those and alert on everything else at medium severity rather than filtering by resource type. Use a two stage approach: first alert on a new identity creating resources at all, then add the rate threshold once you have sixty days of baseline data per account. Feed certificate and domain monitoring into the same queue so that external and internal findings are reviewed together, and give each case a path to a takedown request. The coverage you lose by allowlisting approved roles is a compromised pipeline credential, so add a separate rule for provisioning outside the pipeline schedule and for new access keys created on those roles.
